briefing.headline: The model predicts 12-month departures roughly triple, from 487 to 1,484 of 5,000 employees (about 10% to 30%), or roughly 1,000 extra leavers; treat the scale as directional, not a forecast.
briefing.most_at_risk: Caregivers react worst (+294% leaving vs +177% for those without caring duties), especially those with long commutes, because fixed days plus 60–100 minute commutes collide with school pickup, toddlers and elderly parents, and several say they are already job hunting.
risks: Loss of experienced people, not just new hires: mid-level (+236%) and managers (+223%) rise more than juniors (+187%), and voices with 7–15 years' tenure describe updating résumés.

The badge tracking and VP sign-off are read as distrust even by short-commute employees who could absorb three days, which turns tolerable inconvenience into resentment (average feeling -1.48, near the bottom of the scale) and invites recruiter calls.

The policy falls harder on caregivers and slightly harder on women (+223% vs +205% for men), creating a fairness and reputational exposure. Managers who must enforce badge reviews are themselves at elevated risk of leaving.
design_changes: Drop individual badge-swipe reviews and set team-level attendance expectations instead. The trust signal comes up in almost every voice, including those otherwise willing to comply.
Let each team pick its anchor days rather than imposing company-wide set days, and move exception approval from VPs to direct managers, with published criteria covering caregiving and long commutes.

Extend the 90-day lead time and phase in, for example one or two days first. Pair the rollout with a clear business reason and visible commute or caregiving support, so people decide after seeing it work, not on announcement day.
briefing.confidence: low, because the direction (more exits, worst among caregivers and long commuters) is consistent across groups and voices, but the tripling rests on just 48 modelled voices (two per group), and many voices say they will look rather than leave, so the exact number could be overstated.

subgroup_checks.claim: Bigger rise for mid and senior managers
